Anthony Jeselnik was born on 22 December 1978 in Upper St. Clair, Pennsylvania, USA. He is a writer and producer, known for [Anthony Jeselnik: Thoughts and Prayers (2015)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt5087554/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), [Anthony Jeselnik: Fire in the Maternity Ward (2019)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt10050780/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) and [Night of Too Many Stars: An Overbooked Concert for Autism Education (2010)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt1754273/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk).

Paul Dessau was born on 19 December 1894 in Hamburg, Germany. He was a composer, known for [Adventures of Casanova (1948)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0040075/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), [The Novel of Werther (1938)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0030958/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) and [Never Trust a Woman (1930)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0020993/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk). He was married to [Ruth Berghaus](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm3115318/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), [Antje Ruge](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0749380/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), [Elisabeth Hauptmann](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm1641335/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) and Gudrun Kabisch. He died on 28 June 1979 in Königs Wusterhausen, German Democratic Republic.

[](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0006036/bio/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_sm)

Paul Dessau was born on 19 December 1894 in Hamburg, Germany. He was a composer, known for [Adventures of Casanova (1948)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0040075/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), [The Novel of Werther (1938)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0030958/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) and [Never Trust a Woman (1930)](https://www.imdb.com/title/tt0020993/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk). He was married to [Ruth Berghaus](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm3115318/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), [Antje Ruge](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm0749380/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), [Elisabeth Hauptmann](https://www.imdb.com/name/nm1641335/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) and Gudrun Kabisch. He died on 28 June 1979 in Königs Wusterhausen, German Democratic Republic.

Ivan Finta was born on 1 January 1965 in Zlaté Moravce, Czechoslovakia [now Slovakia]. He is a cinematographer, known for [Polcas rozpadu (2007)](http://www.imdb.com/title/tt1179788/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), [Láska na vlásku (2014)](http://www.imdb.com/title/tt4122590/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) and [Scumbag (2020)](http://www.imdb.com/title/tt11239374/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk).

#### [Fans of the TV show should love it.](http://www.imdb.com/title/tt0345950/reviews/?featured=rw1641421&ref_=tt_ururv_c_1_hd)

Although I'm sure there are many parents who would shudder at the thought of sitting down to watch The Spongebob Squarepants Movie, I was actually looking forward to it: it may be a far cry from the Disney and Hanna-Barbera fodder I was raised on, but I love the surreal and 'anything goes' vibe of the TV programme and was keen to see the feature length version.  
  
The story centres around Spongebob's attempt to retrieve King Neptune's stolen crown, in order to save the life of his boss, Mr. Krabs, who has been framed for the crime. Together with his friend Patrick, Spongebob travels to Shell City to find the crown and save the day.  
  
Spongebob is a well-meaning character who I find it impossible not to like, and although perhaps the format is stretched a tad too far for an hour-and-a-half long film, there is still plenty to enjoy about this fun packed feature (let's face itany film that sees a climactic fight take place on David Hasselhoff's butt, and a sponge defeat evil via the power of rock 'n' roll, has got to be worth seeing!).  
  
The Spongebob Squarepants Movie may not win any new fans, but those who think that the TV show is genius should definitely give this one a whirl.

SpongeBob finally made it to the big screen and the good thing is - it is nothing less of the TV series, just longer and more fun. Staring SpongeBob and Patrick in search of stolen crown of King Neptune, before he turns Mr. Crab into fried crab.  
  
If you're a fan of the TV series this will not disappoint you at all, and if you're not a fan you will become one. Surprisingly, the movie able to bring all the characteristic and style of the show on to the big screen without trying too hard. It is still the same old SpongeBob, and that what I like about this movie.  
  
The story is consistence and the humor is still fun to watch, there is always something new coming up making it unpredictable. And the original song is brilliantly written and somewhat quite inspiring. SpongeBob still make it big despite being a 2D cartoon cause the animation here is colorfully done.  
  
Overall: I enjoy the whole film, but maybe a little downside on the David Hasselhoff parts. But overall it is an extremely enjoyable film.  
  
Reason To Watch: Finally Able To See SpongeBob In Full Length Movie. Triple The Fun.

#### [Fans of the TV show should love it.](http://www.imdb.com/title/tt0345950/reviews/?featured=rw1641421&ref_=tt_ururv_c_1_hd)

Although I'm sure there are many parents who would shudder at the thought of sitting down to watch The Spongebob Squarepants Movie, I was actually looking forward to it: it may be a far cry from the Disney and Hanna-Barbera fodder I was raised on, but I love the surreal and 'anything goes' vibe of the TV programme and was keen to see the feature length version.  
  
The story centres around Spongebob's attempt to retrieve King Neptune's stolen crown, in order to save the life of his boss, Mr. Krabs, who has been framed for the crime. Together with his friend Patrick, Spongebob travels to Shell City to find the crown and save the day.  
  
Spongebob is a well-meaning character who I find it impossible not to like, and although perhaps the format is stretched a tad too far for an hour-and-a-half long film, there is still plenty to enjoy about this fun packed feature (let's face itany film that sees a climactic fight take place on David Hasselhoff's butt, and a sponge defeat evil via the power of rock 'n' roll, has got to be worth seeing!).  
  
The Spongebob Squarepants Movie may not win any new fans, but those who think that the TV show is genius should definitely give this one a whirl.

#### [I was curious why my kid likes Spongebob so much...](http://www.imdb.com/title/tt0345950/reviews/?featured=rw0968519&ref_=tt_ururv_c_2_hd)

I went to see Spongebob because my kid has pretty sophisticated taste, and I couldn't imagine how a cartoon sponge could be interesting. But it was interesting. I wasn't bored for a second, and actually laughed out loud numerous times. Parts of it were definitely off color, but that made it more adult....not just a cartoon kid movie. I loved the David Hasselhof bit. I also liked the other real people and locations that weren't cartoon. This movie would be scary for real little kids, which may help explain why middle school kids like it. I'm not going to watch the TV show every week, but I do think a parent could do worse than going to see Spongebob with his kid...a pleasant afternoon, and insight into what they are watching...

#### [It's SpongeBob, 'nuff said](http://www.imdb.com/title/tt0345950/reviews/?featured=rw1030560&ref_=tt_ururv_c_4_hd)

I didn't quite know what to expect when I walked into the theater to watch the movie of one of my favorite cartoons. Nickelodeon has a really nasty habit of "big-budgtizing" movies of their shows (changing the look, etc.). However this is not the case with SpongeBob. Whew, one less thing to worry about.  
  
Next was the story. Could Steve Hillenburg live up to what had been laid down by the series? Yes. Basically it's like watching a 1 1/2 hour episode of SpongeBob (and who couldn't like that). Lot's of visual gags and typical Sponge brainless-ness. I was quite impressed.  
  
If you're a SpongeBob fan, you'll love this movie. If you're not, eh, watch it anyways, it'll do you good ;-).

#### [Enjoy](http://www.imdb.com/title/tt0345950/reviews/?featured=rw1485156&ref_=tt_ururv_c_5_hd)

SpongeBob finally made it to the big screen and the good thing is - it is nothing less of the TV series, just longer and more fun. Staring SpongeBob and Patrick in search of stolen crown of King Neptune, before he turns Mr. Crab into fried crab.  
  
If you're a fan of the TV series this will not disappoint you at all, and if you're not a fan you will become one. Surprisingly, the movie able to bring all the characteristic and style of the show on to the big screen without trying too hard. It is still the same old SpongeBob, and that what I like about this movie.  
  
The story is consistence and the humor is still fun to watch, there is always something new coming up making it unpredictable. And the original song is brilliantly written and somewhat quite inspiring. SpongeBob still make it big despite being a 2D cartoon cause the animation here is colorfully done.  
  
Overall: I enjoy the whole film, but maybe a little downside on the David Hasselhoff parts. But overall it is an extremely enjoyable film.  
  
Reason To Watch: Finally Able To See SpongeBob In Full Length Movie. Triple The Fun.  
  
Reason Not To: Dislike Real People Acting With Cartoon.  
  
Rating: 7/10 (Grade: B-).

Paul Dessau was born on 19 December 1894 in Hamburg, Germany. He was a composer, known for [Adventures of Casanova (1948)](http://www.imdb.com/title/tt0040075/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), [The Novel of Werther (1938)](http://www.imdb.com/title/tt0030958/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) and [Never Trust a Woman (1930)](http://www.imdb.com/title/tt0020993/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk). He was married to [Ruth Berghaus](http://www.imdb.com/name/nm3115318/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), [Antje Ruge](http://www.imdb.com/name/nm0749380/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), [Elisabeth Hauptmann](http://www.imdb.com/name/nm1641335/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) and Gudrun Kabisch. He died on 28 June 1979 in Königs Wusterhausen, German Democratic Republic.

Paul Dessau was born on 19 December 1894 in Hamburg, Germany. He was a composer, known for [Adventures of Casanova (1948)](http://www.imdb.com/title/tt0040075/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), [The Novel of Werther (1938)](http://www.imdb.com/title/tt0030958/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) and [Never Trust a Woman (1930)](http://www.imdb.com/title/tt0020993/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk). He was married to [Ruth Berghaus](http://www.imdb.com/name/nm3115318/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), [Antje Ruge](http://www.imdb.com/name/nm0749380/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), [Elisabeth Hauptmann](http://www.imdb.com/name/nm1641335/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) and Gudrun Kabisch. He died on 28 June 1979 in Königs Wusterhausen, German Democratic Republic.

Josh Comers is an Emmy-nominated writer and stand-up comedian. Getting his start on The Tonight Show with Conan O'Brien, he subsequently was a staff writer for TBS' CONAN and The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon. Known for his sharp jokes, he has written for numerous Comedy Central Roasts, including those of Alec Baldwin, Bruce Willis, Justin Bieber, James Franco, Charlie Sheen, and David Hasselhoff. He is also a seasoned Awards Show writer and his work on Hulu's Triumph's Election Watch special earned him a Writers Guild of America Award.

Josh Comers is an Emmy-nominated writer and stand-up comedian. Getting his start on The Tonight Show with Conan O'Brien, he subsequently was a staff writer for TBS' CONAN and The Tonight Show Starring Jimmy Fallon. Known for his sharp jokes, he has written for numerous Comedy Central Roasts, including those of Alec Baldwin, Bruce Willis, Justin Bieber, James Franco, Charlie Sheen, and David Hasselhoff. He is also a seasoned Awards Show writer and his work on Hulu's Triumph's Election Watch special earned him a Writers Guild of America Award.

Robert Stolz was born on 25 August 1880 in Graz, Styria, Austria-Hungary [now Austria]. He was a composer and actor, known for [13 Sins (2014)](http://www.imdb.com/title/tt2059171/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), [Spring Parade (1940)](http://www.imdb.com/title/tt0033095/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) and [It Happened Tomorrow (1944)](http://www.imdb.com/title/tt0036962/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk). He was married to Yvonne Louise Ulrich, Josephine Zernitz, Grete Holm, Franzi Ressel and Lilli. He died on 27 June 1975 in West Berlin, West Germany.

Robert Stolz was born on 25 August 1880 in Graz, Styria, Austria-Hungary [now Austria]. He was a composer and actor, known for [13 Sins (2014)](http://www.imdb.com/title/tt2059171/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), [Spring Parade (1940)](http://www.imdb.com/title/tt0033095/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) and [It Happened Tomorrow (1944)](http://www.imdb.com/title/tt0036962/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk). He was married to Yvonne Louise Ulrich, Josephine Zernitz, Grete Holm, Franzi Ressel and Lilli. He died on 27 June 1975 in West Berlin, West Germany.

**Anthony Jeselnik** ([/ˈ dʒ ɛ s əl n ɪ k/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[_JES-əl-nik_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key"); born December 22, 1978)[[1]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-1) is an American comedian, writer, actor, and producer. He is known for his [dark comedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_comedy "Dark comedy") style, which emphasizes ironic misdirection, [non sequiturs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non_sequitur_(literary_device) "Non sequitur (literary device)"), biting insults, an arrogant demeanor, and a [stage persona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stage_persona "Stage persona") that frequently takes [amoral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amorality "Amorality") stances.

Jeselnik was a writer for _[Late Night with Jimmy Fallon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late\_Night\_with\_Jimmy\_Fallon "Late Night with Jimmy Fallon")_ in its first season and hosted a _[Comedy Central Presents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy\_Central\_Presents "Comedy Central Presents")_ in 2009. After releasing his critically acclaimed debut album _[Shakespeare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakespeare\_(album) "Shakespeare (album)")_ in 2010, he began writing for the [Comedy Central Roasts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy_Central_Roasts "Comedy Central Roasts") and moved up to performer in the 2011 roast of [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump"). He continued to perform on the roasts of [Charlie Sheen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Sheen "Charlie Sheen") and [Roseanne Barr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roseanne_Barr "Roseanne Barr") in 2012. In 2013, he hosted his own [Comedy Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy_Central "Comedy Central") series for two seasons, _[The Jeselnik Offensive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Jeselnik\_Offensive "The Jeselnik Offensive")_, and released his second album, _[Caligula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caligula\_(Anthony\_Jeselnik\_album) "Caligula (Anthony Jeselnik album)")_, which doubles as an hour-long stand-up special.

On July 22, 2015, Jeselnik replaced [J. B. Smoove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._B._Smoove "J. B. Smoove") as the new host of [NBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBC "NBC")'s [Emmy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmy_Award "Emmy Award")-nominated series _[Last Comic Standing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last\_Comic\_Standing "Last Comic Standing")_.[[2]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-2) His second stand-up special, _[Thoughts and Prayers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony\_Jeselnik:\_Thoughts\_and\_Prayers "Anthony Jeselnik: Thoughts and Prayers")_, premiered in October 2015 on [Netflix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netflix "Netflix"); his third, _[Fire in the Maternity Ward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony\_Jeselnik:\_Fire\_in\_the\_Maternity\_Ward "Anthony Jeselnik: Fire in the Maternity Ward")_, premiered on Netflix in April 2019; his fourth, _[Bones and All](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony\_Jeselnik:\_Bones\_and\_All?action=edit&redlink=1 "Anthony Jeselnik: Bones and All (page does not exist)")_, premiered on Netflix in November 2024. Jeselnik starred in the first season of the [NFL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Football_League "National Football League") Media podcast _The Rosenthal & Jeselnik Vanity Project_ (or _RJVP_) along with best friend Gregg Rosenthal. The second season debuted in 2018 on the [Comedy Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy_Central "Comedy Central") Podcast Network under the slightly different name of _The Jeselnik & Rosenthal Vanity Project_ (or _JRVP_).

## Early life

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Anthony_Jeselnik&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Anthony Jeselnik grew up the oldest of five children in a Catholic family in [Upper St. Clair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_St._Clair_Township,_Pennsylvania "Upper St. Clair Township, Pennsylvania"), [Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania "Pennsylvania"). His father was a lawyer and his mother a housewife.[[3]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-parade-3)

Jeselnik was interested in making others laugh from an early age. In elementary school, he would often interrupt the class to tell a joke. On one occasion, a classmate was moving to a different town that was not generally regarded well, and Jeselnik cracked a sarcastic comment: "Oh, well, send us a postcard."[[4]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-avclub-4) When the teacher laughed at his joke, he realized: "If you're smart enough that adults get it, you can get away with anything."[[4]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-avclub-4) He would often stay up attempting to watch _[Saturday Night Live](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturday\_Night\_Live "Saturday Night Live")_ and, as he grew older, _[The Ben Stiller Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Ben\_Stiller\_Show "The Ben Stiller Show")_ and _[Mr. Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mr.\_Show "Mr. Show")_.[[4]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-avclub-4)

Jeselnik graduated from [Upper St. Clair High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_St._Clair_High_School "Upper St. Clair High School") in 1997. He earned a bachelor's degree in English literature with a business minor from [Tulane University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulane_University "Tulane University") in 2001. During his senior year at Tulane, his girlfriend accidentally burned down his apartment, which he would later use as early stand-up material.[[4]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-avclub-4) He was a member of the [Alpha Tau Omega](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpha_Tau_Omega "Alpha Tau Omega") fraternity while at [Tulane University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulane_University "Tulane University"). His original dream was to write the [Great American Novel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_American_Novel "Great American Novel"), but an internship in Los Angeles between his junior and senior years of college convinced him there were other avenues for a writer.[[5]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-postgazette-5)

Jeselnik first tried standup in the early 2000s, while in his early 20s, after moving to Los Angeles and taking a day job at a [Borders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borders_(retailer) "Borders (retailer)"). He found a book by writer and comedian Greg Dean that promoted Dean's [Santa Monica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Monica "Santa Monica") comedy workshops.[[6]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-6)[[7]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-grantland-7) In his first attempt at a joke, Jeselnik did an impression of his father being stung by wasps. By the end of the skit—which lasted only one minute, but Jeselnik claimed "felt like 10"—no one had laughed, leading Jeselnik to swear off physical comedy forever.[[4]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-avclub-4) After being fired[_[why?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_] by Borders, he worked behind the scenes as an accounting clerk for the TV series _[Deadwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deadwood\_(TV\_series) "Deadwood (TV series)")_, during which time he would perform at open-mic nights.[[4]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-avclub-4)

Inspired in part by [Mitch Hedberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitch_Hedberg "Mitch Hedberg"), [Dennis Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dennis_Miller "Dennis Miller"), [Sarah Silverman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Silverman "Sarah Silverman"),[[8]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-8) and [Steven Wright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Wright "Steven Wright"), it was two years into his stand-up comedy career when Jeselnik had a "[lightbulb moment](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/light-bulb%20moment "wikt:light-bulb moment")".[[7]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-grantland-7) After writing a bizarre joke with a dark twist to it, the audience response encouraged Jeselnik to focus more in that area. The joke, titled "My Girlfriend Loves to Eat Chocolate", was later featured on _Shakespeare_.[[4]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-avclub-4)[[7]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-grantland-7)

At the [Comedy Cellar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy_Cellar "Comedy Cellar"), Jeselnik was influenced by how comedians derided each other, especially [Jim Norton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Norton_(comedian) "Jim Norton (comedian)"), [Colin Quinn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colin_Quinn "Colin Quinn"), [Bobby Kelly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Kelly "Bobby Kelly"), and [Keith Robinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Robinson_(comedian) "Keith Robinson (comedian)").[[9]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-9)

## Career

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Anthony_Jeselnik&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

Jeselnik's _[Comedy Central Presents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy\_Central\_Presents "Comedy Central Presents")_ stand-up special premiered in 2009, and he was named one of [Comedy Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy_Central "Comedy Central")'s breakout comedians of the year alongside [Nick Kroll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Kroll "Nick Kroll"), [Aziz Ansari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aziz_Ansari "Aziz Ansari"), [Whitney Cummings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitney_Cummings "Whitney Cummings"), [Donald Glover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Glover "Donald Glover"), [Matt Braunger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Braunger "Matt Braunger"), [T. J. Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T._J._Miller "T. J. Miller"), [Kumail Nanjiani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kumail_Nanjiani "Kumail Nanjiani"), and [Jon Lajoie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Lajoie "Jon Lajoie").[[10]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-10) In 2009, Jeselnik was hired as a writer for _[Late Night with Jimmy Fallon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late\_Night\_with\_Jimmy\_Fallon "Late Night with Jimmy Fallon")_. His dream job, predating stand-up or his first comedy class, was to sit around a table and "throw out jokes with people you respected."[[7]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-grantland-7) After getting the job, Jeselnik's pitches would be continually shot down as they were too dark. For example, he routinely fought for a single joke regarding [obesity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obesity "Obesity") each day for a month, and although Fallon liked the joke, he felt uncomfortable performing it as it would likely jeopardize his likability with the obese.[[7]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-grantland-7) During this period, he was a regular at the [Comedy Cellar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy_Cellar "Comedy Cellar") in [Greenwich Village](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenwich_Village "Greenwich Village"), New York City.[[11]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-maron-11) Jeselnik would work hard each day for the show and then proceed to go to Comedy Cellar, have a "big stiff drink", and do his act, feeling "miserable". In March 2010, he approached the show's producers and told them he wanted to leave. "We understand—you want to go be Anthony Jeselnik", they said.[[7]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-grantland-7)

He recorded his debut album, _[Shakespeare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakespeare\_(album) "Shakespeare (album)")_, and in 2010 began writing for the [Comedy Central Roasts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy_Central_Roasts "Comedy Central Roasts"). Jeselnik, who refers to roasts as "the [Super Bowl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl "Super Bowl") of comedy", loved roasts during college and always tried to write for them.[[4]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-avclub-4) While Jeselnik was writing for the [David Hasselhoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Hasselhoff "David Hasselhoff") roast, Comedy Central executives took an interest in him and offered him an opportunity to perform on the next roast. Knowing that this would be his "big moment", Jeselnik refers to the Roast of [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") as "one of my favorite moments of my life [...] because no one knew who I was and it just really caught everybody by surprise. And the next day, my life was completely different."[[4]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-avclub-4) While Jeselnik had previously been headlining clubs, the audience often was unfamiliar with his brand of comedy; after the Trump roast, the crowds got bigger and Jeselnik felt more comfortable.[[4]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-avclub-4) Immediately following his performance, the network offered Jeselnik a "three-point deal" in which one receives an hour special, three Comedy Central roasts, and a development deal.[[7]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-grantland-7) Jeselnik went on to perform at two more roasts, the Comedy Central Roasts of [Charlie Sheen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Sheen "Charlie Sheen") in 2011 and [Roseanne Barr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roseanne_Barr "Roseanne Barr") in 2012.[[7]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-grantland-7)[[12]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-HuffPo-12)[[13]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-13)

Jeselnik appeared at the Power of Comedy event in November 2012.[[14]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-The_Los_Angeles_Times-14)[[15]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-Extra-15)

In 2013, Jeselnik hosted his own [Comedy Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy_Central "Comedy Central") series, _[The Jeselnik Offensive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Jeselnik\_Offensive "The Jeselnik Offensive")_. In preparing the show, Comedy Central was looking for a half-hour, a four-nights-a-week show following _[The Colbert Report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Colbert\_Report "The Colbert Report")_ titled _Midnight_.[[7]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-grantland-7) Jeselnik's main draw was the monologue, where he felt he could tell jokes that he was unable to do on _Late Night with Jimmy Fallon_. For the pilot, Jeselnik did a test interview with a celebrity but felt "so wrong [...] it just fit me like a bad suit."[[4]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-avclub-4) For the show's first episode, Jeselnik performs cancer-related stand-up for a cancer support group. "I had to fight with Comedy Central to put that on the first episode", said Jeselnik. The network felt uneasy using the sketch as an introduction.[[4]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-avclub-4) Jeselnik pointed to the premiere episode of _[Chappelle's Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chappelle's\_Show "Chappelle's Show")_, in which [Dave Chappelle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Chappelle "Dave Chappelle") plays a blind African-American [Klansman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ku_Klux_Klan "Ku Klux Klan"), which he regarded as "one of the edgiest things they ever did." As such, the sketch opened the first episode and received a positive reception; [Jay Leno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jay_Leno "Jay Leno") called to inform Jeselnik "how much he loved the cancer segment."[[4]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-avclub-4)_The Jeselnik Offensive_ ran for two seasons on [Comedy Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy_Central "Comedy Central") from February 19, 2013, to August 27, 2013.

Jeselnik's first stand-up special, _Caligula_, premiered in 2013.[[16]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-16)[[17]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-17)

October 2015 saw the debut of _The Rosenthal & Jeselnik Vanity Project_ (RJVP), a podcast available on NFL.com hosted by Jeselnik and fellow Tulane graduate, NFL Network's Gregg Rosenthal.[[18]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-18)

In 2015 Jeselnik released his critically acclaimed third stand up special, and first for Netflix, _Thoughts and Prayers_.[[19]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-19) The hourlong special offers Jeselnik's trademark dark humor for the first forty minutes and personal anecdotes for the last twenty. He discusses his grandmother's funeral, the [Boston Marathon bombing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Marathon_bombing "Boston Marathon bombing"), the cancelation of _The Jeselnik Offensive_, and the death threats he receives.

In September 2018 Jeselnik returned to Comedy Central, signing a multi-platform development deal which includes new episodes of a weekly podcast, _The Jeselnik & Rosenthal Vanity Project_ (JRVP), where Jeselnik is joined by his friend and NFL Network analyst Gregg Rosenthal, and by producer and NFL Network director Erica Tamposi.[[20]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-20)As of April 2024[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Anthony_Jeselnik&action=edit), over 240 episodes have been released.[[21]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-21)

Jeselnik's fourth stand-up special, _Fire in the Maternity Ward_, was released by Netflix on April 30, 2019.[[22]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-22) This was followed recently by a fifth Netflix special, _Bones and All_, released on November 26, 2024.[[23]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-23)

## Personal life

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Anthony_Jeselnik&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Jeselnik dated comedian [Amy Schumer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amy_Schumer "Amy Schumer") from 2009 until 2011.[[24]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-24)

Jeselnik is an [atheist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atheist "Atheist").[[3]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-parade-3)

He is of [Slovenian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovenes "Slovenes") descent.[[25]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-25)[[26]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-26) He said that he found out online that the surname Jeselnik is Slovenian.

**Anthony Jeselnik** ([/ˈ dʒ ɛ s əl n ɪ k/](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:IPA/English "Help:IPA/English")[_JES-əl-nik_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key"); born December 22, 1978)[[1]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-1) is an American comedian, writer, actor, and producer. He is known for his [dark comedy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dark_comedy "Dark comedy") style, which emphasizes ironic misdirection, [non sequiturs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Non_sequitur_(literary_device) "Non sequitur (literary device)"), biting insults, an arrogant demeanor, and a [stage persona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stage_persona "Stage persona") that frequently takes [amoral](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amorality "Amorality") stances.

Jeselnik was a writer for _[Late Night with Jimmy Fallon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late\_Night\_with\_Jimmy\_Fallon "Late Night with Jimmy Fallon")_ in its first season and hosted a _[Comedy Central Presents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy\_Central\_Presents "Comedy Central Presents")_ in 2009. After releasing his critically acclaimed debut album _[Shakespeare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakespeare\_(album) "Shakespeare (album)")_ in 2010, he began writing for the [Comedy Central Roasts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy_Central_Roasts "Comedy Central Roasts") and moved up to performer in the 2011 roast of [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump"). He continued to perform on the roasts of [Charlie Sheen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Sheen "Charlie Sheen") and [Roseanne Barr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roseanne_Barr "Roseanne Barr") in 2012. In 2013, he hosted his own [Comedy Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy_Central "Comedy Central") series for two seasons, _[The Jeselnik Offensive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Jeselnik\_Offensive "The Jeselnik Offensive")_, and released his second album, _[Caligula](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caligula\_(Anthony\_Jeselnik\_album) "Caligula (Anthony Jeselnik album)")_, which doubles as an hour-long stand-up special.

On July 22, 2015, Jeselnik replaced [J. B. Smoove](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/J._B._Smoove "J. B. Smoove") as the new host of [NBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NBC "NBC")'s [Emmy Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmy_Award "Emmy Award")-nominated series _[Last Comic Standing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Last\_Comic\_Standing "Last Comic Standing")_.[[2]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-2) His second stand-up special, _[Thoughts and Prayers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony\_Jeselnik:\_Thoughts\_and\_Prayers "Anthony Jeselnik: Thoughts and Prayers")_, premiered in October 2015 on [Netflix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netflix "Netflix"); his third, _[Fire in the Maternity Ward](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony\_Jeselnik:\_Fire\_in\_the\_Maternity\_Ward "Anthony Jeselnik: Fire in the Maternity Ward")_, premiered on Netflix in April 2019; his fourth, _[Bones and All](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony\_Jeselnik:\_Bones\_and\_All?action=edit&redlink=1 "Anthony Jeselnik: Bones and All (page does not exist)")_, premiered on Netflix in November 2024. Jeselnik starred in the first season of the [NFL](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National_Football_League "National Football League") Media podcast _The Rosenthal & Jeselnik Vanity Project_ (or _RJVP_) along with best friend Gregg Rosenthal. The second season debuted in 2018 on the [Comedy Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy_Central "Comedy Central") Podcast Network under the slightly different name of _The Jeselnik & Rosenthal Vanity Project_ (or _JRVP_).

## Early life

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Anthony_Jeselnik&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

Anthony Jeselnik grew up the oldest of five children in a Catholic family in [Upper St. Clair](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_St._Clair_Township,_Pennsylvania "Upper St. Clair Township, Pennsylvania"), [Pennsylvania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pennsylvania "Pennsylvania"). His father was a lawyer and his mother a housewife.[[3]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-parade-3)

Jeselnik was interested in making others laugh from an early age. In elementary school, he would often interrupt the class to tell a joke. On one occasion, a classmate was moving to a different town that was not generally regarded well, and Jeselnik cracked a sarcastic comment: "Oh, well, send us a postcard."[[4]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-avclub-4) When the teacher laughed at his joke, he realized: "If you're smart enough that adults get it, you can get away with anything."[[4]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-avclub-4) He would often stay up attempting to watch _[Saturday Night Live](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturday\_Night\_Live "Saturday Night Live")_ and, as he grew older, _[The Ben Stiller Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Ben\_Stiller\_Show "The Ben Stiller Show")_ and _[Mr. Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mr.\_Show "Mr. Show")_.[[4]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-avclub-4)

Jeselnik graduated from [Upper St. Clair High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Upper_St._Clair_High_School "Upper St. Clair High School") in 1997. He earned a bachelor's degree in English literature with a business minor from [Tulane University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulane_University "Tulane University") in 2001. During his senior year at Tulane, his girlfriend accidentally burned down his apartment, which he would later use as early stand-up material.[[4]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-avclub-4) He was a member of the [Alpha Tau Omega](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alpha_Tau_Omega "Alpha Tau Omega") fraternity while at [Tulane University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulane_University "Tulane University"). His original dream was to write the [Great American Novel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_American_Novel "Great American Novel"), but an internship in Los Angeles between his junior and senior years of college convinced him there were other avenues for a writer.[[5]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-postgazette-5)

Jeselnik first tried standup in the early 2000s, while in his early 20s, after moving to Los Angeles and taking a day job at a [Borders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Borders_(retailer) "Borders (retailer)"). He found a book by writer and comedian Greg Dean that promoted Dean's [Santa Monica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Santa_Monica "Santa Monica") comedy workshops.[[6]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-6)[[7]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-grantland-7) In his first attempt at a joke, Jeselnik did an impression of his father being stung by wasps. By the end of the skit—which lasted only one minute, but Jeselnik claimed "felt like 10"—no one had laughed, leading Jeselnik to swear off physical comedy forever.[[4]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-avclub-4) After being fired[_[why?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Please\_clarify "Wikipedia:Please clarify")_] by Borders, he worked behind the scenes as an accounting clerk for the TV series _[Deadwood](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deadwood\_(TV\_series) "Deadwood (TV series)")_, during which time he would perform at open-mic nights.[[4]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-avclub-4)

Inspired in part by [Mitch Hedberg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mitch_Hedberg "Mitch Hedberg"), [Dennis Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dennis_Miller "Dennis Miller"), [Sarah Silverman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sarah_Silverman "Sarah Silverman"),[[8]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-8) and [Steven Wright](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steven_Wright "Steven Wright"), it was two years into his stand-up comedy career when Jeselnik had a "[lightbulb moment](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/light-bulb%20moment "wikt:light-bulb moment")".[[7]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-grantland-7) After writing a bizarre joke with a dark twist to it, the audience response encouraged Jeselnik to focus more in that area. The joke, titled "My Girlfriend Loves to Eat Chocolate", was later featured on _Shakespeare_.[[4]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-avclub-4)[[7]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-grantland-7)

At the [Comedy Cellar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy_Cellar "Comedy Cellar"), Jeselnik was influenced by how comedians derided each other, especially [Jim Norton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jim_Norton_(comedian) "Jim Norton (comedian)"), [Colin Quinn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colin_Quinn "Colin Quinn"), [Bobby Kelly](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bobby_Kelly "Bobby Kelly"), and [Keith Robinson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Keith_Robinson_(comedian) "Keith Robinson (comedian)").[[9]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-9)

## Career

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Anthony_Jeselnik&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

Jeselnik's _[Comedy Central Presents](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy\_Central\_Presents "Comedy Central Presents")_ stand-up special premiered in 2009, and he was named one of [Comedy Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy_Central "Comedy Central")'s breakout comedians of the year alongside [Nick Kroll](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nick_Kroll "Nick Kroll"), [Aziz Ansari](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aziz_Ansari "Aziz Ansari"), [Whitney Cummings](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Whitney_Cummings "Whitney Cummings"), [Donald Glover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Glover "Donald Glover"), [Matt Braunger](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Braunger "Matt Braunger"), [T. J. Miller](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/T._J._Miller "T. J. Miller"), [Kumail Nanjiani](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kumail_Nanjiani "Kumail Nanjiani"), and [Jon Lajoie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Lajoie "Jon Lajoie").[[10]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-10) In 2009, Jeselnik was hired as a writer for _[Late Night with Jimmy Fallon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late\_Night\_with\_Jimmy\_Fallon "Late Night with Jimmy Fallon")_. His dream job, predating stand-up or his first comedy class, was to sit around a table and "throw out jokes with people you respected."[[7]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-grantland-7) After getting the job, Jeselnik's pitches would be continually shot down as they were too dark. For example, he routinely fought for a single joke regarding [obesity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Obesity "Obesity") each day for a month, and although Fallon liked the joke, he felt uncomfortable performing it as it would likely jeopardize his likability with the obese.[[7]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-grantland-7) During this period, he was a regular at the [Comedy Cellar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy_Cellar "Comedy Cellar") in [Greenwich Village](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Greenwich_Village "Greenwich Village"), New York City.[[11]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-maron-11) Jeselnik would work hard each day for the show and then proceed to go to Comedy Cellar, have a "big stiff drink", and do his act, feeling "miserable". In March 2010, he approached the show's producers and told them he wanted to leave. "We understand—you want to go be Anthony Jeselnik", they said.[[7]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-grantland-7)

He recorded his debut album, _[Shakespeare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shakespeare\_(album) "Shakespeare (album)")_, and in 2010 began writing for the [Comedy Central Roasts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy_Central_Roasts "Comedy Central Roasts"). Jeselnik, who refers to roasts as "the [Super Bowl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Super_Bowl "Super Bowl") of comedy", loved roasts during college and always tried to write for them.[[4]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-avclub-4) While Jeselnik was writing for the [David Hasselhoff](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Hasselhoff "David Hasselhoff") roast, Comedy Central executives took an interest in him and offered him an opportunity to perform on the next roast. Knowing that this would be his "big moment", Jeselnik refers to the Roast of [Donald Trump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Donald_Trump "Donald Trump") as "one of my favorite moments of my life [...] because no one knew who I was and it just really caught everybody by surprise. And the next day, my life was completely different."[[4]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-avclub-4) While Jeselnik had previously been headlining clubs, the audience often was unfamiliar with his brand of comedy; after the Trump roast, the crowds got bigger and Jeselnik felt more comfortable.[[4]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-avclub-4) Immediately following his performance, the network offered Jeselnik a "three-point deal" in which one receives an hour special, three Comedy Central roasts, and a development deal.[[7]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-grantland-7) Jeselnik went on to perform at two more roasts, the Comedy Central Roasts of [Charlie Sheen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlie_Sheen "Charlie Sheen") in 2011 and [Roseanne Barr](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roseanne_Barr "Roseanne Barr") in 2012.[[7]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-grantland-7)[[12]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-HuffPo-12)[[13]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-13)

Jeselnik appeared at the Power of Comedy event in November 2012.[[14]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-The_Los_Angeles_Times-14)[[15]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-Extra-15)

In 2013, Jeselnik hosted his own [Comedy Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy_Central "Comedy Central") series, _[The Jeselnik Offensive](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Jeselnik\_Offensive "The Jeselnik Offensive")_. In preparing the show, Comedy Central was looking for a half-hour, a four-nights-a-week show following _[The Colbert Report](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Colbert\_Report "The Colbert Report")_ titled _Midnight_.[[7]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-grantland-7) Jeselnik's main draw was the monologue, where he felt he could tell jokes that he was unable to do on _Late Night with Jimmy Fallon_. For the pilot, Jeselnik did a test interview with a celebrity but felt "so wrong [...] it just fit me like a bad suit."[[4]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-avclub-4) For the show's first episode, Jeselnik performs cancer-related stand-up for a cancer support group. "I had to fight with Comedy Central to put that on the first episode", said Jeselnik. The network felt uneasy using the sketch as an introduction.[[4]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-avclub-4) Jeselnik pointed to the premiere episode of _[Chappelle's Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chappelle's\_Show "Chappelle's Show")_, in which [Dave Chappelle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Chappelle "Dave Chappelle") plays a blind African-American [Klansman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ku_Klux_Klan "Ku Klux Klan"), which he regarded as "one of the edgiest things they ever did." As such, the sketch opened the first episode and received a positive reception; [Jay Leno](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jay_Leno "Jay Leno") called to inform Jeselnik "how much he loved the cancer segment."[[4]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-avclub-4)_The Jeselnik Offensive_ ran for two seasons on [Comedy Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy_Central "Comedy Central") from February 19, 2013, to August 27, 2013.

Jeselnik's first stand-up special, _Caligula_, premiered in 2013.[[16]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-16)[[17]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-17)

October 2015 saw the debut of _The Rosenthal & Jeselnik Vanity Project_ (RJVP), a podcast available on NFL.com hosted by Jeselnik and fellow Tulane graduate, NFL Network's Gregg Rosenthal.[[18]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-18)

In 2015 Jeselnik released his critically acclaimed third stand up special, and first for Netflix, _Thoughts and Prayers_.[[19]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-19) The hourlong special offers Jeselnik's trademark dark humor for the first forty minutes and personal anecdotes for the last twenty. He discusses his grandmother's funeral, the [Boston Marathon bombing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Marathon_bombing "Boston Marathon bombing"), the cancelation of _The Jeselnik Offensive_, and the death threats he receives.

In September 2018 Jeselnik returned to Comedy Central, signing a multi-platform development deal which includes new episodes of a weekly podcast, _The Jeselnik & Rosenthal Vanity Project_ (JRVP), where Jeselnik is joined by his friend and NFL Network analyst Gregg Rosenthal, and by producer and NFL Network director Erica Tamposi.[[20]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-20)As of April 2024[[update]](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Anthony_Jeselnik&action=edit), over 240 episodes have been released.[[21]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-21)

Jeselnik's fourth stand-up special, _Fire in the Maternity Ward_, was released by Netflix on April 30, 2019.[[22]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-22) This was followed recently by a fifth Netflix special, _Bones and All_, released on November 26, 2024.[[23]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-23)

## Personal life

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Anthony_Jeselnik&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Personal life")]

Jeselnik dated comedian [Amy Schumer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amy_Schumer "Amy Schumer") from 2009 until 2011.[[24]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-24)

Jeselnik is an [atheist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Atheist "Atheist").[[3]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-parade-3)

He is of [Slovenian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Slovenes "Slovenes") descent.[[25]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-25)[[26]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthony_Jeselnik#cite_note-26) He said that he found out online that the surname Jeselnik is Slovenian.

Eduardo Abbas was born on 25 May 1930 in São José do Rio Preto, São Paulo, Brazil. He was an actor and production manager, known for [A Gata (1964)](http://www.imdb.com/title/tt0205640/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), [Cavalo Amarelo (1980)](http://www.imdb.com/title/tt0209576/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) and [As Ninfas Insaciáveis (1981)](http://www.imdb.com/title/tt0261108/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk). He died on 16 March 1992 in São Paulo, São Paulo, Brazil.

Eduardo Abbas was born on 25 May 1930 in São José do Rio Preto, São Paulo, Brazil. He was an actor and production manager, known for [A Gata (1964)](http://www.imdb.com/title/tt0205640/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk), [Cavalo Amarelo (1980)](http://www.imdb.com/title/tt0209576/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk) and [As Ninfas Insaciáveis (1981)](http://www.imdb.com/title/tt0261108/?ref_=nm_ov_bio_lk). He died on 16 March 1992 in São Paulo, São Paulo, Brazil.

**Alfred Ernest Jean III** (born January 9, 1961) is an American screenwriter and producer.[[1]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-1) Jean is well known for his work on _[The Simpsons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Simpsons "The Simpsons")_. He was raised near [Detroit](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit "Detroit"), Michigan, and graduated from [Harvard University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University") in 1981. Jean began his writing career in the 1980s with fellow Harvard alum [Mike Reiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Reiss "Mike Reiss"). Together, they worked as writers and producers on television shows such as _[The Tonight Show Starring Johnny Carson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Tonight\_Show\_Starring\_Johnny\_Carson "The Tonight Show Starring Johnny Carson")_, _[ALF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ALF\_(TV\_series) "ALF (TV series)")_ and _[It's Garry Shandling's Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's\_Garry\_Shandling's\_Show "It's Garry Shandling's Show")_.

Jean was offered a job as a writer on the animated sitcom _The Simpsons_ in 1989, alongside Reiss, and together they became the first members of the show's original writing staff. They served as [showrunners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Showrunner "Showrunner") during the show's third (1991–92) and fourth (1992–93) seasons, though they left _The Simpsons_ after season four to create _[The Critic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Critic\_(TV\_series) "The Critic (TV series)")_, an animated show about film critic [Jay Sherman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jay_Sherman "Jay Sherman"). It was first broadcast on [ABC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Broadcasting_Company "American Broadcasting Company") in January 1994 (then aired its second season on [Fox](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fox_Broadcasting_Company "Fox Broadcasting Company") in March 1995) and was well received by critics, but did not catch on with viewers and only lasted for two seasons.

In 1994, Jean and Reiss signed a three-year development deal with [The Walt Disney Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Walt_Disney_Company "The Walt Disney Company") to produce other television shows for ABC. Among multiple pitches made by the duo, their sole project with ABC to come to fruition was the live-action sitcom _[Teen Angel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teen\_Angel\_(1997\_TV\_series) "Teen Angel (1997 TV series)")_, which was cancelled in its first season. Jean returned full-time to _The Simpsons_ during the tenth season (1998–99). He became showrunner again with the start of the thirteenth season in 2001, without Reiss, and he stayed in that position until season thirty-three, where he shared it with [Matt Selman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Selman "Matt Selman") until season thirty-seven, where he stepped down from that position entirely.[[2]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-2) Jean was also one of the writers and producers who worked on _[The Simpsons Movie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Simpsons\_Movie "The Simpsons Movie")_, a feature-length film based on the series, released in 2007.

## Early life

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Al_Jean&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life")]

> "At college, I was privileged to meet and work with some very talented writers who went on to work for _[Saturday Night Live](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saturday\_Night\_Live "Saturday Night Live")_, _[Seinfeld](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seinfeld "Seinfeld")_, _[Late Night with David Letterman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Late\_Night\_with\_David\_Letterman "Late Night with David Letterman")_ and _[The Simpsons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Simpsons "The Simpsons")_. No doubt my exposure to them at a very young age has been enormously helpful to my writing career."

—Jean on his time at [Harvard University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard_University "Harvard University")[[3]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-AWN-3)

Alfred Ernest Jean III was born in [Detroit, Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Detroit,_Michigan "Detroit, Michigan") on January 9, 1961.[[4]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-emleg-4) He was raised in [Farmington Hills, Michigan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Farmington_Hills,_Michigan "Farmington Hills, Michigan"),[[4]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-emleg-4)[[5]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-CT-5) graduated from [Harrison High School](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harrison_High_School_(Michigan) "Harrison High School (Michigan)"), and is of Irish ancestry.[[6]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-NPR-6) After working at his father's hardware store,[[7]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-avc-7) Jean arrived at Harvard University when he was sixteen years old and graduated in 1981[[8]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-PlainDealer-8) with a [bachelor's degree](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bachelor's_degree "Bachelor's degree") in mathematics.[[9]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-9) Daryl Libow, one of Jean's freshman roommates, said he was a "math whiz" when he arrived at Harvard but "soon blossomed and found his comedic feet."[[10]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-Teller-10) In [Holworthy Hall](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holworthy_Hall "Holworthy Hall") at Harvard, Jean met fellow freshman [Mike Reiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Reiss "Mike Reiss"); they befriended one another and collaborated in their writing efforts for the humor publication _[Harvard Lampoon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Harvard\_Lampoon "Harvard Lampoon")_. [Jeff Martin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jeff_Martin_(writer) "Jeff Martin (writer)"), another writer for the _Lampoon_, said "they definitely loomed large around the magazine. They were very funny guys and unusually polished comedy writers for that age. We were never surprised that they went on to success."[[10]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-Teller-10) Jean has also stated that the duo spent most of their time at the _Lampoon_, adding that "it was practically my second dorm room."[[10]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-Teller-10) He eventually became vice-president of the publication.[[3]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-AWN-3)

## Career

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Al_Jean&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

### Early career and _The Simpsons_

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Al_Jean&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: Early career and The Simpsons")]

The humor magazine _[National Lampoon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/National\_Lampoon\_(magazine) "National Lampoon (magazine)")_ hired Jean and Reiss after they graduated in 1981.[[10]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-Teller-10) During the 1980s, the duo began collaborating on various television material.[[11]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-Tampa-11)[[12]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-MJ-12) During this period, they worked as writers and producers on television shows such as _[The Tonight Show Starring Johnny Carson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Tonight\_Show\_Starring\_Johnny\_Carson "The Tonight Show Starring Johnny Carson")_, _[ALF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/ALF\_(TV\_series) "ALF (TV series)")_, _[Sledge Hammer!](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sledge\_Hammer! "Sledge Hammer!")_ and _[It's Garry Shandling's Show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It's\_Garry\_Shandling's\_Show "It's Garry Shandling's Show")_.[[3]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-AWN-3)[[13]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-TDB-13) In 1989, Jean was offered a job as a writer on the animated sitcom _[The Simpsons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Simpsons "The Simpsons")_,[[14]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-Washington-14) a show created by [Matt Groening](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Groening "Matt Groening"), [James L. Brooks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_L._Brooks "James L. Brooks") and [Sam Simon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sam_Simon "Sam Simon") that continues to air today.[[6]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-NPR-6) Many of Jean's friends were not interested in working on _The Simpsons_ because it was a cartoon and they did not think it would last long.[[13]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-TDB-13) Jean, however, was a fan of the work of Groening, Brooks and Simon, and therefore took the job together with Reiss.[[6]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-NPR-6)[[13]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-TDB-13)

The duo became the first members of the original _Simpsons_ writing staff and worked on the thirteen episodes of the series' [first season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Simpsons_season_1 "The Simpsons season 1") (1989–90).[[13]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-TDB-13) While watching the [first episode of the show](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pilot_episode "Pilot episode"), "[Simpsons Roasting on an Open Fire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simpsons_Roasting_on_an_Open_Fire "Simpsons Roasting on an Open Fire")", premiering on television in December 1989, Jean opined to himself that the series was the greatest project he had been involved with and desired to continue working on it for the rest of his professional career.[[6]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-NPR-6) What he enjoyed most about _The Simpsons_ at the time was something he recognized from Brooks' previous work: although the show was largely based on humor, it had depth and warmth.[[6]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-NPR-6)

[![Image 6](http://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/1/17/Mikereiss.jpg/250px-Mikereiss.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mikereiss.jpg)

[Mike Reiss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Reiss "Mike Reiss") and Jean worked as [show runners](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Show_runner "Show runner") of _The Simpsons_ together.

Although Jean has been credited as the sole writer of several episodes, he considers the process to be mainly collaborative: "the principal writer [of an episode] has, at most, written 40% of the script. It's a real team effort."[[13]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-TDB-13) The writer credited in the episode's [opening credits](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Opening_credits "Opening credits") is the person that came up with the idea for the episode and wrote the first draft, even if he or she only contributed to a small part of the final script.[[13]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-TDB-13) Jean has stated that [Lisa Simpson](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisa_Simpson "Lisa Simpson") is one of his favorite characters to write for.[[15]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-IGN1-15) She is the character he relates to the most because of their similar childhoods and the fact that he has a daughter.[[16]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-UGO-16)

Jean became [showrunner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Showrunner "Showrunner") of _The Simpsons_ at the start of the third season (1991–92) together with Reiss.[[16]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-UGO-16) A showrunner has the ultimate responsibility of all the processes that an episode goes through before completion, including the writing, the animation, the voice acting and the music.[[13]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-TDB-13) According to Jean, when he began his tenure as showrunner, the only thing he thought to himself every day was "Don't blow it and screw up this thing everyone loves."[[16]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-UGO-16) The first episode Jean and Reiss ran was "[Mr. Lisa Goes to Washington](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mr._Lisa_Goes_to_Washington "Mr. Lisa Goes to Washington")" (aired September 26, 1991), and they felt pressured to make it good, so much so that they did six to seven rewrites of the script in order to improve its humor. Jean said he "kept thinking 'It's not good enough. It's not good enough.'"[[17]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-JeanWashington-17) Reiss added that "we were definitely scared. We had never run anything before, and they dumped us on this."[[18]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-Reiss-18)

Jean and Reiss served as showrunners until the end of the fourth season in 1993.[[17]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-JeanWashington-17) Since the show had already established itself in the first two seasons, they were able to give it more depth during their tenure. Jean believes this is one of the reasons that many fans and critics regard season three and four as the best seasons of _The Simpsons_.[[16]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-UGO-16)[Bill Oakley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bill_Oakley "Bill Oakley"), another _Simpsons_ writer, has commented that "Mike and Al are responsible for the best thing that ever appeared on television, which was the third season of _The Simpsons_."[[10]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-Teller-10) Comedy writer [Jay Kogen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jay_Kogen "Jay Kogen") has said that "those years with Al Jean and Mike Reiss running it were pretty darn good. And then the ones after that maybe not so much. Some people ran it better than others."[[19]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-19)

### _The Critic_ and Disney

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Al_Jean&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: The Critic and Disney")]

[![Image 7](http://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/8/81/Mirkinjean.jpg/250px-Mirkinjean.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Mirkinjean.jpg)

Jean and former _Simpsons_ executive producer [David Mirkin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Mirkin "David Mirkin") at the 2007 [Comic Con](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Diego_Comic-Con_International "San Diego Comic-Con International").

Jean and Reiss left _The Simpsons_ after its [fourth season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Simpsons_season_4 "The Simpsons season 4") in order to create _[The Critic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Critic\_(TV\_series) "The Critic (TV series)")_, an animated show about film critic [Jay Sherman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jay_Sherman "Jay Sherman") (voiced by [Jon Lovitz](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jon_Lovitz "Jon Lovitz")); the show was executive produced by Brooks.[[20]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-feare-20)[[21]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-21) It was first broadcast on [ABC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Broadcasting_Company "American Broadcasting Company") in January 1994 and was well received by critics,[[22]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-22)[[23]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-23) but did not catch on with viewers and was put on hiatus after six weeks. It returned in June 1994 and completed airing its initial production run.[[24]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-returns-24)_The Critic_ was moved to the [Fox network](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fox_network "Fox network") for its second season.[[25]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-25) Since _The Simpsons_ also aired on that network, Brooks was able to create a [crossover](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fictional_crossover "Fictional crossover") between it and _The Critic._[[26]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-LATimes-26)

Said crossover occurred through the _Simpsons_ episode "[A Star Is Burns](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/A_Star_Is_Burns "A Star Is Burns")" (1995). Groening was not fond of the crossover, publicly citing it as a thirty-minute advertisement for _The Critic_.[[26]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-LATimes-26) Brooks said, "for years, Al and Mike were two guys who worked their hearts out on this show, staying up until 4 in the morning to get it right. The point is, Matt's name has been on Mike's and Al's scripts and he has taken plenty of credit for a lot of their great work. In fact, he is the direct beneficiary of their work. _The Critic_ is their shot and he should be giving them his support." Reiss stated that he was a "little upset" by Groening's actions and that "this taints everything at the last minute. [...] This episode doesn't say 'Watch _The Critic_' all over it."[[26]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-LATimes-26) Jean added "What bothers me about all of this, is that now people may get the impression that this _Simpsons_ episode is less than good. It stands on its own even if _The Critic_ never existed."[[26]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-LATimes-26) On Fox, _The Critic_ was again short-lived, broadcasting ten episodes before its cancellation. A total of only 23 episodes were produced, and it returned briefly in 2000 with a series of ten Internet broadcast [webisodes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Webisode "Webisode"). The series has since developed a [cult following](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cult_following "Cult following") thanks to reruns on [Comedy Central](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Comedy_Central "Comedy Central") and its complete series release on [DVD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DVD "DVD").[[27]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-Slant-27)

In 1994, Jean and Reiss signed a three-year deal with [The Walt Disney Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Walt_Disney_Company "The Walt Disney Company") to produce other television shows for ABC. The duo created and executive produced _[Teen Angel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Teen\_Angel\_(1997\_TV\_series) "Teen Angel (1997 TV series)")_, which was canceled in its first season. Reiss said "It was so compromised and overworked. I had 11 executives full-time telling me how to do my job."[[28]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-bristol-28) The pair periodically returned to work on _The Simpsons_— for example, while under contract at Disney they were allowed to write and produce four episodes of the show, including [season eight](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Simpsons_season_8 "The Simpsons season 8")'s "[Simpsoncalifragilisticexpiala(Annoyed Grunt)cious](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simpsoncalifragilisticexpiala(Annoyed_Grunt)cious "Simpsoncalifragilisticexpiala(Annoyed Grunt)cious")" (1997).[[29]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-calif-29)

### Further work on _The Simpsons_

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Al_Jean&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Further work on The Simpsons")]

> "What has defined the Al Jean era is the show's definitive move into the mainstream of American TV and culture. By now _The Simpsons_ is the most successful show in the history of television—it's a long way from the young, mouthy, experimental series on the upstart network [Fox]. With the show's popularity such a shift was inevitable, and for many reasons it's unfair to compare today's episodes with those from the show's heyday."

—John Ortved in _[The Simpsons: An Uncensored, Unauthorized History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Simpsons:\_An\_Uncensored,\_Unauthorized\_History "The Simpsons: An Uncensored, Unauthorized History")_[[30]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-30)

Following _Teen Angel'_ s cancellation, Jean and Reiss ceased their writing partnership. Subsequently, Jean alone returned full-time to _The Simpsons_ during the [tenth season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Simpsons_season_10 "The Simpsons season 10") (1998–99)[[6]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-NPR-6) and became a prominent writer and executive producer during the ensuing three seasons, all produced under [Mike Scully](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Scully "Mike Scully")'s supervision. Following Scully's departure in 2001, Jean returned to the showrunner position with the start of the [thirteenth season](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Simpsons_season_13 "The Simpsons season 13") (2001–2002),[[17]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-JeanWashington-17) likewise without Reiss.[[13]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-TDB-13) Jean called it "a great job with a lot of responsibility," and cited "the fact that people love it so much" as "great."[[16]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-UGO-16) He adds, however, that "the hardest thing at this point is just thinking of fresh ideas. People are so on top of things that we've done before, so the challenge now is to think of an idea that's good, but hasn't been seen."[[13]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-TDB-13) Jean's return was initially welcomed, with [MSNBC](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/MSNBC "MSNBC")'s Jon Bonné stating: "Jean, who took the show's helm from executive producer [Mike Scully](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mike_Scully "Mike Scully") in 2001, has guided the show away from its gag-heavy, Homer-centric incarnation...these are certainly brighter days for the show's long-time fans."[[31]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-Back-31) However, some critics have argued that the show's quality has continued to decline in recent years during Jean's tenure. Jean has responded to this criticism by saying: "Well, it's possible that we've declined. But honestly, I've been here the whole time and I do remember in season two people saying, 'It's gone downhill.' If we'd listened to that then we would have stopped after [episode 13](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Homer_vs._Lisa_and_the_8th_Commandment "Homer vs. Lisa and the 8th Commandment"). I'm glad we didn't."[[32]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-32)

Jean was one of the writers and producers who worked on _[The Simpsons Movie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Simpsons\_Movie "The Simpsons Movie")_, a feature-length film released in 2007.[[15]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-IGN1-15) The show's voice cast was signed on to do the film in 2001,[[33]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-empire-33) and work then began on the script.[[34]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-usa-34) The _Simpsons_ producers were initially worried that creating a film would have a negative effect on the show, as they did not have enough crew to focus their attention on both projects. As the show progressed, additional writers and animators were hired so that both the show and the film could be produced at the same time.[[35]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-officialsite-35) Groening and Brooks were therefore able to invite Jean (who continued to work as show runner on the television show) to produce the film with them.[[36]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-pig_feces-36)

Jean frequently appears on the _Simpsons_ DVD [audio commentaries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Audio_commentary "Audio commentary") for episodes which he has collaborated on. He told [IGN](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IGN "IGN") that he enjoys doing them because he has not seen some of the episodes in ten to fifteen years, and "it's kind of like a reunion to see some of the people that I worked with before, so it's a really pleasant experience."[[15]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-IGN1-15)

From 2020 to 2025, he was joint showrunner with [Matt Selman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matt_Selman "Matt Selman"), running four to six episodes per season himself beginning with season thirty-three. Jean has also co-written and produced a number of Simpsons shorts, including: _[The Longest Daycare](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Longest\_Daycare "The Longest Daycare")_, nominated for the [Academy Award for Best Animated Short Film](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_Award_for_Best_Animated_Short_Film "Academy Award for Best Animated Short Film"); _[The Force Awakens from Its Nap](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Force\_Awakens\_from\_Its\_Nap "The Force Awakens from Its Nap")_ and _[When Billie Met Lisa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/When\_Billie\_Met\_Lisa "When Billie Met Lisa")_, which were both nominated for the [Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Short Form Animated Program](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Primetime_Emmy_Award_for_Outstanding_Short_Form_Animated_Program "Primetime Emmy Award for Outstanding Short Form Animated Program"); and _[The Simpsons | Balenciaga](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The\_Simpsons\_Balenciaga "The Simpsons Balenciaga")_, which won the 2022 [Clio Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clio_Awards "Clio Awards") for Film - Scripted.[[37]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-37)

In November 2025, Jean announced that he would step down as showrunner of the show after serving for nearly 25 years in the role. The last episode where he served as showrunner was the episode "[Bad Boys... for Life?](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bad_Boys..._for_Life%3F "Bad Boys... for Life?")", which was written by him. Selman took over the full showrunning duties afterwards, while Jean remains on the show as a writer and consulting producer.[[38]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-38)

## Awards

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Al_Jean&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: Awards")]

Jean has received ten [Emmy Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Emmy_Award "Emmy Award")[[39]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-emmy-39) and two [Peabody Awards](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peabody_Award "Peabody Award") for his work on _The Simpsons_.[[3]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-AWN-3)[[13]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-TDB-13) In 1997, he and Reiss won an [Annie Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Annie_Award "Annie Award") in the "Best Producing in a TV Production" category for the _Simpsons_ episode "[The Springfield Files](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Springfield_Files "The Springfield Files")".[[40]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-A25-40) In 1991 they shared the Writing A Comedy Series CableAce Award for the It's Garry Shandling's Show Episode "My Mother The Wife". In 2006, the duo was given the Animation Writers Caucus Animation Award which is given by the [Writers Guild of America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Writers_Guild_of_America "Writers Guild of America") to writers that "advanced the literature of animation in film and/or television through the years and who has made outstanding contributions to the profession of the animation writer."[[41]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-41)

## Personal life

[[edit](http://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Al_Jean&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: Personal life")]

As of 2005, Jean lives in [Los Angeles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Los_Angeles "Los Angeles"), California, with his wife,[[5]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-CT-5) television writer [Stephanie Gillis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stephanie_Gillis "Stephanie Gillis").[[42]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-42) Jean also has two daughters.[[11]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-Tampa-11)[[43]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-Seattle-43)[[44]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-Advertiser-44)[[45]](http://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Al_Jean#cite_note-45)
